Forces’ withdrawal from Iraq and Afghanistan after a decade of war and the demand for deep cuts in government spending including defense spending under the government’s serious fiscal situation, the guidance was developed to review defense priorities and present a blueprint for the Joint Force in

[4981] In the new Defense Strategic Guidance, the Obama Administration articulated a policy that would place the Asia-Pacific region at the focus of U. S. strategy, including the security strategy (Rebalancing to the Asia-Pacific Region

[4982] Furthermore, in March 2014 the Administration published the Quadrennial Defense Review (QDR), the second review since President Obama took office

[4983] The 2014 QDR builds on the 2012 Defense Strategic Guidance and embodies the priorities outlined in it, including rebalancing to the Asia-Pacific region, indicating that the Obama Administration continues to place an emphasis on the region

[4984] Meanwhile, as the growing budget deficits of the U. S. government in recent years have called for deep cuts in spending, in January 2012 the Department of Defense announced that the reduction in defense spending will amount to about 487 billion dollars over the 10 years from FY2012 to FY

[4999] Quadrennial Defense Review (QDR

[5000] In March 2014, the Department of Defense released the Quadrennial Defense Review (QDR

[5001] The QDR outlines policies concerning U. S. Forces' capabilities and composition in anticipation of the security environment of the next 20 years

[5002] The United States Code mandates that the Secretary of Defense submits the QDR to the Congress every four years

[5003] The 2014 QDR builds on the 2012 Defense Strategic Guidance and embodies the priorities outlined in it

[5004] Understanding of Security The 2014 QDR states that the future international security environment remains uncertain and complicated due to the shifting international balance of power; the greater interaction between states, non-state entities and private citizens; the proliferation of technology; and the rapidly accelerating spread of information

[5005] In addressing this challenging environment, the QDR states that the United States collaborates with allies and partners to accomplish a wide range of goals, and leverages the technological and human capital strengths of the U.S. Forces

[5006] The QDR recognizes that the Asia-Pacific region is increasingly central to global commerce, politics and security

[5007] At the same time, the report points out that defense expenditure in the region continues to rise and countries within the region continue to enhance their military and security capabilities, bringing greater risk that tensions arising from long-standing sovereign disputes or claims to natural resources will spur disruptive competition or erupt into conflict

[5008] In particular, it notes that the rapid pace and comprehensive scope of China’s military modernization continues, combined with a relative lack of transparency and openness regarding both military capabilities and intentions

[5009] In relation to North Korea, the review says that its long-range missile and weapons of mass destruction (WMD) programs, particularly its pursuit of nuclear weapons in violation of international obligations, constitutes a significant threat to peace and stability on the Korean Peninsula and Northeast Asia and is a growing, direct threat to the United States

[5010] As for the Middle East, the report suggests that the sectarian divide is among the sources of transnational division, while competition for resources will worsen tensions and could escalate into broader conflicts, particularly in fragile states

[5011] The report states that Iran remains a destabilizing actor that threatens security by defying international law and pursuing capabilities that would allow it to develop nuclear weapons

[5012] Even as Iran pledges not to pursue nuclear Authority of the Prime Minister for Response Measures Following the stipulation of the Basic Response Plan, for overall promotion of response measures, the Task Force for Armed Attack Situations, etc., (the Task Force) will be established within the Cabinet, with the Prime Minister appointed as leader of the Task Force and appropriate Ministers of State as Deputy Chief and other members of the Task Force

[5013] If the Prime Minister recognizes that there are obstacles to protecting the lives, bodies, and properties of the people, and to eliminating an armed attack, when necessary response measures under comprehensive coordination are not implemented, he may instruct the head of the local government concerned and other relevant persons to implement the necessary measures

[5014] In circumstances where necessary response measures are not implemented or if there is an obstacle weapons, its other destabilizing activities including development of mid- and long-range missiles and support to terrorists and insurgents, will continue to pose a threat to the security of the Middle East and the U. S. allies and partners

[5015] Furthermore, it states that as countries in the Middle East and Africa undergo political and social change, terrorist groups seek to expand their influence, and internal strife in Syria has become a magnet for global jihad, bringing ongoing spillover effects including an influx of foreign fighters and a flood of refugees into neighboring countries

[5016] In Africa, it mentions that terrorists, criminal organizations and pirates exploit ungoverned and undergoverned territory, causing potential for rapidly developing threats, particularly of terrorist attacks in fragile states, that could pose acute challenges to U. S. interests

[5017] The report says that Europe remains the principal partner in promoting global security, particularly in addressing challenges such as persistent unrest and violence in the Middle East and North Africa

[5018] The QDR states that while the United States is willing to undertake security cooperation with Russia, both in the bilateral context and in seeking solutions to regional challenges, Russia’s multidimensional defense modernization and actions that violate the sovereignty of neighbors present risks and thus the United States will engage Russia to increase transparency and reduce the risk of military miscalculation

[5019] Concerning the global trends, the report refers to the emergence of international partners with the capacity to play security roles in their respective regions, as well as international cooperation and shared norms of behavior at unprecedented levels of global interconnectedness

[5020] At the same time it also states that the spread and proliferation of technology offers new tools for state and non-state adversaries such as terrorists to pursue asymmetric approaches in the 21st century operational environment

[5021] Furthermore, the report states that in coming years, countries such as China will continue seeking to counter U.S. strengths using anti-access and area-denial (A2/AD) approaches and by employing other new cyber and space control technologies

[5022] It also says that elements such as cyberspace, space, sophisticated technology, WMD, terrorism and climate change poses additional challenges

[5023] The 2014 QDR emphasizes the following three pillars, which are interdependent and mutually reinforcing, in order to embody priorities outlined in the 2012 Defense Strategic Guidance including rebalancing toward the Asia-Pacific region and strong commitment to stability in Europe and the Middle East

[5024] Protect the Homeland: Maintain the capability to deter and defeat attacks on the United States

[5025] Protection of the homeland includes assisting U.S. civil authorities in protecting U.S. airspace, shores, and borders, and in responding effectively to domestic disasters

[5026] Build security globally: Continue a strong U. S. commitment to shaping world events in order to deter and prevent conflict and to assure the allies and partners of the shared security

[5027] Project power and win decisively: the U. S. Forces deter acts of aggression in one or more theaters by remaining capable of decisively defeating adversaries, while projecting power to provide humanitarian assistance and disaster relief

[5028] The QDR states that across the three pillars, the U. S. Forces are capable of simultaneously implementing the following undertakings, and if deterrence fails at any given time, U. S. forces could defeat a regional adversary in a large-scale multi-phased campaign, and deny the objectives of—or imposing unacceptable costs on—another aggressor in another region

[5029] Defending homeland 2) Conducting sustained, distributed counterterrorist operations

[5030] Deterring aggression and assuring allies through forward presence and engagement in multiple regions

[5031] Furthermore, in order to achieve the three pillars, the Department of Defense seeks innovative approaches to how to fight, how to posture the force, and how to leverage the asymmetric strengths and technological advantages

[5032] More specifically, the QDR mentions positioning additional forward-deployed naval forces in critical areas, such as the Asia-Pacific region, and deploying new combinations of ships, aviation assets, and crisis response forces

[5033] Rebalancing of the Joint Force Given major changes in the U.S. security environment including geopolitical changes, changes in modern warfare, and changes in the fiscal environment, the 2014 QDR states that the Department of Defense will rebalance the Joint Force for a broad spectrum of conflict, rebalance and maintain the presence and posture abroad, and rebalance capability, capacity and readiness

[5034] The QDR also says that while the force will become smaller, it will become more modern as well, with readiness improving

[5035] Furthermore, it states that particularly in an era of reduced budget and other resources, the Department will redouble its efforts to protect key capability areas listed below, that are most closely aligned to the pillars of the defense strategy

[5036] Missile defense: Increase the number of Ground-Based Interceptors and build depth into the sensor network

[5037] Deploy a second radar in Japan that will improve early warning and tracking of any missiles launched by North Korea

[5038] Increase defense interceptor reliability and effectiveness to improve discrimination capabilities, and to establish a more robust sensor network

[5039] Study the best location in the United States for an additional missile defense interceptor site

[5040] Nuclear deterrence: Continue to invest in modernizing the essential nuclear delivery systems, warheads, command and control, and nuclear weapon infrastructure

[5041] Develop the Cyber Mission Force that operates and defends the Department networks and supports military operations worldwide by

[5296] Following the end of the Cold War, the leaders of Japan and the United States announced the Japan–U. S. Joint Declaration on Security in 1996, reaffirming the importance of the Japan–U. S. Alliance in light of the state of affairs in the Asia-Pacific region following the Cold War

[5297] Upon the Declaration, the final report was compiled at the Special Action Committee on Okinawa (SACO) at the end of that year, and as part of the promotion of cooperative relations presented in the Declaration, at the Japan-U. S. Alliance’s capacity more effective to adapt to changing times

S. Forces in Japan, in May

[5318] “2+2” Meeting (October

[5319] On October 3, 2013, Japan and the United States held the “2+2” Meeting in Tokyo

[5320] This “2+2” Meeting was the historic meeting where all the four Ministers in charge of foreign affairs and defense of Japan and the United States got together in Tokyo for the first time and demonstrated the direction of strengthening the Japan-U. S. Alliance at home and overseas

[5321] At the meeting, while sharing anew the perception of the changing security environment in the Asia-Pacific region, Japan and the United States, with shared values, set forth a strategic vision from the medium- to long-term perspectives in order to achieve a more robust Japan-U. S. Alliance

[5322] The major achievement in the Joint Statement of the latest “2+2” Meeting includes the agreement to complete the review of the current Guidelines by the end of 2014; the agreement to further enhance and deepen bilateral security and defense cooperation, including in such areas as cyberspace and space, and to strengthen regional cooperation, including trilateral cooperation with Australia and the Republic of Korea; and regarding the realignment of the U. S. Forces stationed in Japan, the underscoring of the strong determination toward the relocation of MCAS Futenma to Camp Schwab and the agreement to steadily implement the previous agreements as early as possible and also to address a variety of new measures from the perspective of mitigating the impact on Okinawa

[5350] Direction of Strengthening the Alliance

[5351] As described in the previous section, the Joint Statement of the “2+2” Meeting in October 2013 covered joint intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance (ISR) activities, joint training and exercises, joint/shared use of facilities, cooperation in cyberspace, etc. as the contents of bilateral security and defense cooperation in order to ensure the Alliance’s credibility into the future

[5352] The new National Defense Program Guidelines also incorporated many items of bilateral security and defense cooperation set forth in the Joint Statement as part of the strengthening of the Japan-U.S. Alliance’s deterrence and response capabilities as well as cooperating in a broad range of areas

[5353] It is important to strengthen the Japan-U. S. Alliance through these initiatives not only for ensuring Japan’s security but also for the peace and stability of the international community, including the Asia-Pacific region

[5354] Strengthening of the Japan-U. S. Alliance’s Deterrence and Response Capabilities The new National Defense Program Guidelines state that in order to strengthen the deterrence and response capabilities of the Japan-U. S. Alliance, Japan will build seamless cooperation with the United States ranging from situations in peacetime to various situations, including cooperation in responding to “gray-zone” situations, while increasing the presence of Japan and the United States in the western Pacific region

[5355] To that end, as part of specific cooperation measures in peacetime, Japan and the United States continue to promote joint training and exercises, and joint ISR activities, as well as joint/shared use of facilities and areas of the two countries as a basis for these activities

[5356] The synergy effects of these three elements of cooperative initiatives can further strengthen and improve the operational efficiency of the SDF and the U.S. Forces, including efficiency, interoperability, readiness, mobility, and sustainability

[5449] Quadrennial Defense Review (QDR

[5450] In March 2014, the Department of Defense released the Quadrennial Defense Review (QDR

[5451] The QDR outlines policies concerning U. S. Forces' capabilities and composition in anticipation of the security environment of the next 20 years

[5452] The United States Code mandates that the Secretary of Defense submits the QDR to the Congress every four years

[5453] The 2014 QDR builds on the 2012 Defense Strategic Guidance and embodies the priorities outlined in it

[5454] The 2014 QDR states that the future international security environment remains uncertain and complicated due to the shifting international balance of power; the greater interaction between states, non-state entities and private citizens; the proliferation of technology; and the rapidly accelerating spread of information

[5455] In addressing this challenging environment, the QDR states that the United States collaborates with allies and partners to accomplish a wide range of goals, and leverages the technological and human capital strengths of the U.S. Forces

[5456] The QDR recognizes that the Asia-Pacific region is increasingly central to global commerce, politics and security

[5457] At the same time, the report points out that defense expenditure in the region continues to rise and countries within the region continue to enhance their military and security capabilities, bringing greater risk that tensions arising from longstanding sovereign disputes or claims to natural resources will spur disruptive competition or erupt into conflict

[5458] In particular, it notes that the rapid pace and comprehensive scope of China’s military modernization continues, combined with a relative lack of transparency and openness regarding both military capabilities and intentions

[5459] In relation to North Korea, the review says that its long-range missile and weapons of mass destruction (WMD) programs, particularly its pursuit of nuclear weapons in violation of international obligations, constitutes a significant threat to peace and stability on the Korean Peninsula and Northeast Asia and is a growing, direct threat to the United States

[5460] As for the Middle East, the report suggests that the sectarian divide is among the sources of trans-national division, while competition for resources will worsen tensions and could escalate into broader conflicts, particularly in fragile states

[5461] The report states that Iran remains a destabilizing actor that threatens security by defying international law and pursuing capabilities that would allow it to develop nuclear weapons

[5462] Even as Iran pledges not to pursue nuclear weapons, its other destabilizing activities including development of mid- and long-range missiles and support to terrorists and insurgents, will continue to pose a threat to the security of the Middle East and the U. S. allies and partners

[5463] Furthermore, it states that as countries in the Middle East and Africa undergo political and social change, terrorist groups seek to expand their influence, and internal strife in Syria has become a magnet for global jihad, bringing ongoing spillover effects including an influx of foreign fighters and a flood of refugees into neighboring countries

[5464] In Africa, it mentions that terrorists, criminal organizations and pirates exploit ungoverned and undergoverned territory, causing potential for rapidly developing threats, particularly of terrorist attacks in fragile states, that could pose acute challenges to U. S. interests

[5465] The report says that Europe remains the principal partner in promoting global security, particularly in addressing challenges such as persistent unrest and violence in the Middle East and North Africa

[5466] The QDR states that while the United States is willing to undertake security cooperation with Russia, both in the bilateral context and in seeking solutions to regional challenges, Russia’s multidimensional defense modernization and actions that violate the sovereignty of neighbors present risks and thus the United States will engage Russia to increase transparency and reduce the risk of military miscalculation

[5467] Concerning the global trends, the report refers to the emergence of international partners with the capacity to play security roles in their respective regions, as well as international cooperation and shared norms of behavior at unprecedented levels of global interconnectedness

[5468] At the same time it also states that the spread and proliferation of technology offers new tools for state and non-state adversaries such as terrorists to pursue asymmetric approaches in the 21st century operational environment

[5469] Furthermore, the report states that in coming years, countries such as China will continue seeking to counter U.S. strengths using anti-access and area-denial (A2/AD) approaches and by employing other new cyber and space control technologies

[5470] It also says that elements such as cyberspace, space, sophisticated technology, WMD, terrorism and climate change poses additional challenges

[5471] The 2014 QDR emphasizes the following three pillars, which are interdependent and mutually reinforcing, in order to embody priorities outlined in the 2012 Defense Strategic Guidance including rebalancing toward the Asia-Pacific region and strong commitment to stability in Europe and the Middle East

[5472] Protect the Homeland

[5473] Maintain the capability to deter and defeat attacks on the United States

[5474] Protection of the homeland includes assisting U.S. civil authorities in protecting U.S. airspace, shores, and borders, and in responding effectively to domestic disasters

[5475] Build security globally: Continue a strong U. S. commitment to shaping world events in order to deter and prevent conflict and to assure the allies and partners of the shared security

[5476] Project power and win decisively: the U. S. Forces deter acts of aggression in one or more theaters by remaining capable of decisively defeating adversaries, while projecting power to provide humanitarian assistance and disaster relief

[5477] The QDR states that across the three pillars, the U. S. Forces are capable of simultaneously implementing the following undertakings, and if deterrence fails at any given time, U. S. forces could defeat a regional adversary in a large-scale multi-phased campaign, and deny the objectives of—or imposing unacceptable costs on—another aggressor in another region

[5478] Defending homeland; 2) Conducting sustained, distributed counterterrorist operations; 3) Deterring aggression and assuring allies through forward presence and engagement in multiple regions

[5479] Furthermore, in order to achieve the three pillars, the Department of Defense seeks innovative approaches to how to fight, how to posture the force, and how to leverage the asymmetric strengths and technological advantages

[5480] More specifically, the QDR mentions positioning additional forward-deployed naval forces in critical areas, such as the Asia-Pacific region, and deploying new combinations of ships, aviation assets, and crisis response forces

[5481] Rebalancing of the Joint Force Given major changes in the U. S. security environment including geopolitical changes, changes in modern warfare, and changes in the fiscal environment, the 2014 QDR states that the Department of Defense will rebalance the Joint Force for a broad spectrum of conflict, rebalance and maintain the presence and posture abroad, and rebalance capability, capacity and readiness

[5482] The 2010 QDR stated that the U. S. Forces possess the capability of countering attacks by two countries while also being able to conduct a wide range of operations

[5483] The 2012 Defense Strategic Guidance states that the United States maintain forces that are able to fully deny a capable state’s aggressive objectives in one region while being capable of denying the objectives of – or imposing unacceptable costs on – an opportunistic aggressor in a second region

[5484] The QDR also says that while the force will become smaller, it will become more modern as well, with readiness improving

[5485] Furthermore, it states that particularly in an era of budget and other resources, the Department will redouble its efforts to protect key capability areas listed below, that are most closely aligned to the pillars of the defense strategy

[5486] Missile defense: Increase the number of Ground-Based Interceptors and build depth into the sensor network

[5487] Deploy a second radar in Japan that will improve early warning and tracking of any missiles launched by North Korea

[5488] Increase defense interceptor reliability and effectiveness to improve discrimination capabilities, and to establish a more robust sensor network

[5489] Study the best location in the United States for an additional missile defense interceptor site

[5490] Nuclear deterrence: Continue to invest in modernizing the essential nuclear delivery systems, warheads, command and control, and nuclear weapon infrastructure

[5491] Develop the Cyber Mission Force that operates and defends the Department networks and supports military operations worldwide by

[5492] In addition, the Department migrates its information systems to a common, Defense-wide network infrastructure known as the Joint Information Environment

[5493] Space: Diversify and expand the coverage of Space Situational Awareness (SSA) through international partnerships

[5494] In the near-term, investment in technology demonstrations and capabilities required to evolve toward more resilient architectures

[5495] Additionally, accelerate initiatives to counter adversary space capabilities including adversary intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance (ISR), and space-enabled precision strike

[5496] See Part I, Chapter 2, Section 4-1 (Outer Space and Security) 5) Air/sea: Invest in combat aircraft, including fighters and long-range strike, survivable persistent surveillance, resilient architectures, and undersea warfare to increase the Joint Force's ability to counter A2/AD challenges

[5497] Deepen collaboration with key allies and partners as they develop future forces and capabilities to counter more sophisticated aggressors

[5498] Precision strike: The Air Forces will procure air-to-surface missiles that allow both fighter and bomber aircraft to engage a wide range of targets effectively, even when the enemy’s air defenses have not been fully suppressed

[5499] The Navy is developing a new, joint, long-range anti-ship cruise missile, which will improve the Joint Force's ability to engage surface combatants in defended airspace

[5500] Intelligence, Surveillance and Reconnaissance (ISR): Rebalance investments toward systems that will be effective in defended airspace and denied areas, in the wake of the drawdown of forces from Iraq and Afghanistan and in light of growing challenges from state adversaries

[5501] Make critical space based systems more resilient by expanding the access to commercial and allied space ISR systems

[5670] The MV-22 is an aircraft that combines vertical takeoff/landing and hovering functions of rotary-wing aircraft on one hand and the speed and range of fixed-wing aircraft on the other

[5671] As the main force of air components of the U.S. Marine Corps, MV-22 aircraft play an important role in engaging in a broad range of activities, including transportation of personnel and goods

[5672] The U. S. Marine Corps is in the process of replacing rotary-wing airplanes (CH-46) with MV-22s, which have superior basic performance

[5673] In June 2011, the Department of Defense announced the replacement of CH-46s deployed at MCAS Futenma with MV-22s

[5674] On June 29, 2012, the U. S. Government made a Host Nation Notification that 12 CH-46s of one squadron in Futenma would be replaced by 12 MV-22s and that CH-46s of the second squadron would be replaced by MV-22s in the summer of

[5675] Following the U. S. announcement and notification, the MOD officials explained measures to ensure safety to Okinawa Prefecture and Iwakuni City

[5676] The movement of the first and the second squadron to MCAS Futenma was completed in October 2012 and in September 2013, respectively

[5677] The MV-22 is a highly capable aircraft; compared with the CH-46, it can fly twice as fast, can carry three times the payload, and has four times the range

[5678] Its deployment to Okinawa will strengthen the deterrence of the U. S. Forces in Japan as a whole and greatly contribute to the peace and stability of the region

[5679] Safety of the MV-22 Osprey After the crash of an MV-22 in Morocco in April 2012 and the crash of a CV-22 in Florida in June 2012, concerns about its safety have grown among Japanese people

[5680] In response, the Government of Japan and the Government of the United States agreed to refrain from any flight operation in Japan until the results of the accident investigation are provided and the safety of flight operation is reconfirmed

[5681] Additionally, in order to confirm its safety, a Japanese analysis and assessment team was set up to validate the contents of the accident investigations of the U. S. government, based on Japan’s own viewpoints and knowledge

[5682] The team examined the investigation results and confirmed that the accident in which the MV-22 crashed in Morocco and the CV-22 crashed in Florida were caused largely by human factors and that there were no safety problems with the aircraft itself

[5683] The MV-22 is designed for the U. S. Marine Corps for assault landing transportation missions, while the CV-22 is designed for the U. S. Air Force aimed at special operations, etc

[5684] Furthermore, to maximize the safety of MV-22 flight operations, the two governments discussed matters concerning operations and measures to prevent accident recurrence at the Japan–U. S. Joint Committee and other occasions

[5685] At the Japan–U. S. Joint Committee, both sides confirmed that measures have been taken to address these human factors in light of the lessons learned from the accidents and agreed to implement specific measures to ensure the safety of MV-22 operations in Japan

[5686] Based on the above, considering that the safety of MV-22 operations in Japan is fully confirmed, the Government of Japan released “On MV-22 Osprey Deployment to Okinawa” on September 19, 2012, and then flight operation of the MV-22 Osprey was started in Japan

[5687] Since then, the Government of Japan recognizes that the U. S. has been in full compliance with the Joint Committee agreement concerning the MV-22 and is operating the MV-22 with maximum consideration for safety

[5688] Furthermore, in order to ensure that full consideration is given to local residents and the Joint Committee agreement is properly implemented, the Government of Japan has been continuously engaging with the U. S. side through various opportunities, including the Japan-U. S. Defense Ministerial Meetings

[5689] Usability of MV-22 Osprey in Case of Disaster In the aftermath of the devastating typhoon that hit the central Philippines in November 2013, 14 MV-22 Osprey aircraft, deployed in Okinawa, were dispatched for humanitarian assistance and disaster relief activities to support “Operation Damayan”

[5690] The MV-22 combines the vertical takeoff/landing and hovering functions of rotary-wing aircraft on the one hand, and the speed and range of fixed-wing aircraft on the other

[5691] Provided its unique capabilities, MV-22s were deployed promptly to affected areas that are difficult to access, and it can transport several hundred isolated victims and about six tons of support goods in a day

[5815] The 2014 QDR states that the future international security environment remains uncertain and complicated due to the shifting international balance of power; the greater interaction between states, non-state entities and private citizens; the proliferation of technology; and the rapidly accelerating spread of information

[5816] In addressing this challenging environment, the QDR states that the United States collaborates with allies and partners to accomplish a wide range of goals, and leverages the technological and human capital strengths of the U. S. Forces

[5817] The QDR recognizes that the Asia-Pacific region is increasingly central to global commerce, politics and security

[5818] At the same time, the report points out that defense expenditure in the region continues to rise and countries within the region continue to enhance their military and security capabilities, bringing greater risk that tensions arising from long-standing sovereign disputes or claims to natural resources will spur disruptive competition or erupt into conflict

[5819] In particular, it notes that the rapid pace and comprehensive scope of China’s military modernization continues, combined with a relative lack of transparency and openness regarding both military capabilities and intentions

[5820] In relation to North Korea, the review says that its long-range missile and weapons of mass destruction (WMD) programs, particularly its pursuit of nuclear weapons in violation of international obligations, constitutes a significant threat to peace and stability on the Korean Peninsula and Northeast Asia and is a growing, direct threat to the United States

[5821] As for the Middle East, the report suggests that the sectarian divide is among the sources of trans-national division, while competition for resources will worsen tensions and could escalate into broader conflicts, particularly in fragile states

[5822] The report states that Iran remains a destabilizing actor that threatens security by defying international law and pursuing capabilities that would allow it to develop nuclear weapons

[5823] Even as Iran pledges not to pursue nuclear weapons, its other destabilizing activities including development of mid- and long-range missiles and support to terrorists and insurgents, will continue to pose a threat to the security of the Middle East and the U. S. allies and partners

[5824] Furthermore, it states that as countries in the Middle East and Africa undergo political and social change, terrorist groups seek to expand their influence, and internal strife in Syria has become a magnet for global jihad, bringing ongoing spillover effects including an influx of foreign fighters and a flood of refugees into neighboring countries

[5825] In Africa, it mentions that terrorists, criminal organizations and pirates exploit ungoverned and under-governed territory, causing potential for rapidly developing threats, particularly of terrorist attacks in fragile states, that could pose acute challenges to U.S. interests

[5826] The report says that Europe remains the principal partner in promoting global security, particularly in addressing challenges such as persistent unrest and violence in the Middle East and North Africa

[5827] The QDR states that while the United States is willing to undertake security cooperation with Russia, both in the bilateral context and in seeking solutions to regional challenges, Russia’s multidimensional defense modernization and actions that violate the sovereignty of neighbors present risks and thus the United States will engage Russia to increase transparency and reduce the risk of military miscalculation

[5828] Concerning the global trends, the report refers to the emergence of international partners with the capacity to play security roles in their respective regions, as well as international cooperation and shared norms of behavior at unprecedented levels of global interconnectedness

[5829] At the same time it also states that the spread and proliferation of technology offers new tools for state and non-state adversaries such as terrorists to pursue asymmetric approaches in the 21st century operational environment

[5830] Furthermore, the report states that in coming years, countries such as China will continue seeking to counter U.S. strengths using anti-access and area-denial (A2/AD) approaches and by employing other new cyber and space control technologies

[5831] It also says that elements such as cyberspace, space, sophisticated technology, WMD, terrorism and climate change poses additional challenges

[5832] The 2014 QDR emphasizes the following three pillars, which are interdependent and mutually reinforcing, in order to embody priorities outlined in the 2012 Defense Strategic Guidance including rebalancing toward the Asia-Pacific region and strong commitment to stability in Europe and the Middle East

[5833] Protect the Homeland: Maintain the capability to deter and defeat attacks on the United States

[5834] Protection of the homeland includes assisting U.S. civil authorities in protecting U. S. airspace, shores, and borders, and in responding effectively to domestic disasters

[5835] Build security globally: Continue a strong U. S. commitment to shaping world events in order to deter and prevent conflict and to assure the allies and partners of the shared security

[5836] Project power and win decisively: the U. S. Forces deter acts of aggression in one or more theaters by remaining capable of decisively defeating adversaries, while projecting power to provide humanitarian assistance and disaster relief

[5837] The QDR states that across the three pillars, the U. S. Forces are capable of simultaneously implementing the following undertakings, and if deterrence fails at any given time, U. S. forces could defeat a regional adversary in a large scale multi-phased campaign, and deny the objectives of—or imposing unacceptable costs on—another aggressor in another region

[5838] Defending homeland 2) Conducting sustained, distributed counterterrorist operations

[5839] Deterring aggression and assuring allies through forward presence and engagement in multiple regions

[5840] Furthermore, in order to achieve the three pillars, the Department of Defense seeks innovative approaches to how to fight, how to posture the force, and how to leverage the asymmetric strengths and technological advantages

[6002] Quadrennial Defense Review (QDR

[6003] In March 2014, the Department of Defense released the Quadrennial Defense Review (QDR

[6004] The QDR outlines policies concerning U. S. Forces' capabilities and composition in anticipation of the security environment of the next 20 years

[6005] The United States Code mandates that the Secretary of Defense submits the QDR to the Congress every four years

[6006] The 2014 QDR builds on the 2012 Defense Strategic Guidance and embodies the priorities outlined in it

[6007] The 2014 QDR states that the future international security environment remains uncertain and complicated due to the shifting international balance of power; the greater interaction between states, non-state entities and private citizens; the proliferation of technology; and the rapidly accelerating spread of information

[6008] In addressing this challenging environment, the QDR states that the United States collaborates with allies and partners to accomplish a wide range of goals, and leverages the technological and human capital strengths of the U.S. Forces

[6009] The QDR recognizes that the Asia-Pacific region is increasingly central to global commerce, politics and security

[6010] At the same time, the report points out that defense expenditure in the region continues to rise and countries within the region continue to enhance their military and security capabilities, bringing greater risk that tensions arising from long-standing sovereign disputes or claims to natural resources will spur disruptive competition or erupt into conflict

[6011] In particular, it notes that the rapid pace and comprehensive scope of China’s military modernization continues, combined with a relative lack of transparency and openness regarding both military capabilities and intentions

[6012] In relation to North Korea, the review says that its long range missile and weapons of mass destruction (WMD) programs, particularly its pursuit of nuclear weapons in violation of international obligations, constitutes a significant threat to peace and stability on the Korean Peninsula and Northeast Asia and is a growing, direct threat to the United States

[6013] As for the Middle East, the report suggests that the sectarian divide is among the sources of trans-national division, while competition for resources will worsen tensions and could escalate into broader conflicts, particularly in fragile states

[6014] The report states that Iran remains a destabilizing actor that threatens security by defying international law and pursuing capabilities that would allow it to develop nuclear weapons

[6015] Even as Iran pledges not to pursue nuclear weapons, its other destabilizing activities including development of mid- and long-range missiles and support to terrorists and insurgents, will continue to pose a threat to the security of the Middle East and the U. S. allies and partners

[6016] Furthermore, it states that as countries in the Middle East and Africa undergo political and social change, terrorist groups seek to expand their influence, and internal strife in Syria has become a magnet for global jihad, bringing ongoing spillover effects including an influx of foreign fighters and a flood of refugees into neighboring countries

[6017] In Africa, it mentions that terrorists, criminal organizations and pirates exploit ungoverned and undergoverned territory, causing potential for rapidly developing threats, particularly of terrorist attacks in fragile states, that could pose acute challenges to U. S. interests

[6018] The report says that Europe remains the principal partner in promoting global security, particularly in addressing challenges such as persistent unrest and violence in the Middle East and North Africa

[6019] The QDR states that while the United States is willing to undertake security cooperation with Russia, both in the bilateral context and in seeking solutions to regional challenges, Russia’s multidimensional defense modernization and actions that violate the sovereignty of neighbors present risks and thus the United States will engage Russia to increase transparency and reduce the risk of military miscalculation

[6020] Concerning the global trends, the report refers to the emergence of international partners with the capacity to play security roles in their respective regions, as well as international cooperation and shared norms of behavior at unprecedented levels of global interconnectedness

[6021] At the same time it also states that the spread and proliferation of technology offers new tools for state and non-state adversaries such as terrorists to pursue asymmetric approaches in the 21st century operational environment

[6022] Furthermore, the report states that in coming years, countries such as China will continue seeking to counter U.S. strengths using anti-access and area-denial (A2/AD) approaches and by employing other new cyber and space control technologies

[6023] It also says that elements such as cyberspace, space, sophisticated technology, WMD, terrorism and climate change pose additional challenges

[6024] The 2014 QDR emphasizes the following three pillars, which are interdependent and mutually reinforcing, in order to embody priorities outlined in the 2012 Defense Strategic Guidance including rebalancing toward the Asia-Pacific region and strong commitment to stability in Europe and the Middle East

[6025] Protect the Homeland

[6026] Maintain the capability to deter and defeat attacks on the United States

[6027] Protection of the homeland includes assisting U.S. civil authorities in protecting U. S. airspace, shores, and borders, and in responding effectively to domestic disasters

[6028] Build security globally: Continue a strong U. S. commitment to shaping world events in order to deter and prevent conflict and to assure the allies and partners of the shared security

[6029] Project power and win decisively: the U. S. Forces deter acts of aggression in one or more theaters by remaining capable of decisively defeating adversaries, while projecting power to provide humanitarian assistance and disaster relief

[6030] The QDR states that across the three pillars, the U. S. Forces are capable of simultaneously implementing the following undertakings, and if deterrence fails at any given time, U. S. forces could defeat a regional adversary in a large-scale multiphased campaign, and deny the objectives of—or imposing unacceptable costs on—another aggressor in another region

[6032] Deterring aggression and assuring allies through forward presence and engagement in multiple regions

[6034] More specifically, the QDR mentions positioning additional forward-deployed naval forces in critical areas, such as the Asia-Pacific region, and deploying new combinations of ships, aviation assets, and crisis response forces

[6035] Rebalancing of the Joint Force Given major changes in the U. [6036] The QDR also says that while the force will become smaller, it will become more modern as well, with readiness improving

[6073] Nuclear Strategy While U. S. President Obama aims to realize a world without nuclear weapons, he notes that this will not be realized in the near future, and indicates the need to maintain a nuclear deterrent as long as nuclear weapons exist

[6074] The Nuclear Posture Review (NPR), which was released in April 2010, indicates that the nuclear security environment is changing and nuclear terrorism and nuclear proliferation are an imminent threat today

[6075] Furthermore, it points to the necessity of working on the issue of ensuring strategic stability with existing nuclear powers, in particular Russia and China

[6076] The NPR presents five key objectives based on awareness of this security environment: preventing nuclear proliferation and nuclear terrorism; reducing the role of U. S. nuclear weapons; maintaining strategic deterrence and stability at reduced nuclear force levels; strengthening regional deterrence and reassuring U. S. allies and partners; and sustaining a safe, secure, and effective nuclear arsenal

[6077] In June 2013, U. S. President Obama delivered a speech on the reduction of nuclear weapons in Berlin, which was then followed by the release of the Report on Nuclear Employment Strategy by the Department of Defense on the same day

[6078] The report revealed U. S. intentions to negotiate with Russia to pursue up to a one-third reduction in deployed strategic nuclear weapons

[6306] Quadrennial Defense Review (QDR

[6307] In March 2014, the Department of Defense released the Quadrennial Defense Review (QDR

[6308] The QDR outlines policies concerning U. S. Forces' capabilities and composition in anticipation of the security environment of the next 20 years

[6309] The United States Code mandates that the Secretary of Defense submits the QDR to the Congress every four years

[6310] The 2014 QDR builds on the 2012 Defense Strategic Guidance and embodies the priorities outlined in it

[6311] The 2014 QDR states that the future international security environment remains uncertain and complicated due to the shifting international balance of power; the greater interaction between states, non-state entities and private citizens; the proliferation of technology; and the rapidly accelerating spread of information

[6312] In addressing this challenging environment, the QDR states that the United States collaborates with allies and partners to accomplish a wide range of goals, and leverages the technological and human capital strengths of the U.S. Forces

[6313] The QDR recognizes that the Asia-Pacific region is increasingly central to global commerce, politics and security

[6314] At the same time, the report points out that defense expenditure in the region continues to rise and countries within the region continue to enhance their military and security capabilities, bringing greater risk that tensions arising from long-standing sovereign disputes or claims to natural resources will spur disruptive competition or erupt into conflict

[6315] In particular, it notes that the rapid pace and comprehensive scope of China’s military modernization continues, combined with a relative lack of transparency and openness regarding both military capabilities and intentions

[6316] In relation to North Korea, the review says that its long-range missile and weapons of mass destruction (WMD) programs, particularly its pursuit of nuclear weapons in violation of international obligations, constitutes a significant threat to peace and stability on the Korean Peninsula and Northeast Asia and is a growing, direct threat to the United States

[6317] As for the Middle East, the report suggests that the sectarian divide is among the sources of transnational division, while competition for resources will worsen tensions and could escalate into broader conflicts, particularly in fragile states

[6318] The report states that Iran remains a destabilizing actor that threatens security by defying international law and pursing capabilities that would allow it to develop nuclear weapons

[6319] Even as Iran pledges not to pursue nuclear weapons on board a Japanese ship provided certain requirements are met, allowing them to carry small arms for the purpose of security operations

[6334] In Africa, it mentions that terrorists, criminal organizations and pirates exploit ungoverned and under-governed territory, causing potential for rapidly developing threats, particularly of terrorist attacks in fragile states, that could pose acute challenges to U.S. interests

[6345] Build security globally: Continue a strong U. S. commitment to shaping world events in order to deter and prevent conflict and to assure the allies and partners of the shared security

[6346] Project power and win decisively: The U.S. Forces deter acts of aggression in one or more theaters by remaining capable of decisively defeating adversaries, while projecting power to provide humanitarian assistance and disaster relief

[6399] Quadrennial Defense Review (QDR

[6400] In March 2014, the Department of Defense released the Quadrennial Defense Review (QDR

[6401] The QDR outlines policies concerning U. S. Forces' capabilities and composition in anticipation of the security environment of the next 20 years

[6402] The United States Code mandates that the Secretary of Defense submits the QDR to the Congress every four years

[6403] The 2014 QDR builds on the 2012 Defense Strategic Guidance and embodies the priorities outlined in it

[6404] The 2014 QDR states that the future international security environment remains uncertain and complicated due to the shifting international balance of power; the greater interaction between states, non-state entities and private citizens; the proliferation of technology; and the rapidly accelerating spread of information

[6405] In addressing this challenging environment, the QDR states that the United States collaborates with allies and partners to accomplish a wide range of goals, and leverages the technological and human capital strengths of the U.S. Forces

[6406] The QDR recognizes that the Asia-Pacific region is increasingly central to global commerce, politics and security

[6407] At the same time, the report points out that defense expenditure in the region continues to rise and countries within the region continue to enhance their military and security capabilities, bringing greater risk that tensions arising from long-standing sovereign disputes or claims to natural resources will spur disruptive competition or erupt into conflict

[6408] In particular, it notes that the rapid pace and comprehensive scope of China’s military modernization continues, combined with a relative lack of transparency and openness regarding both military capabilities and intentions

[6409] In relation to North Korea, the review says that its long-range missile and weapons of mass destruction (WMD) programs, particularly its pursuit of nuclear weapons in violation of international obligations, constitutes a significant threat to peace and stability on the Korean Peninsula and Northeast Asia and is a growing, direct threat to the United States

[6410] As for the Middle East, the report suggests that the sectarian divide is among the sources of trans-national division, while competition for resources will worsen tensions and could escalate into broader conflicts, particularly in fragile states

[6411] The report states that Iran remains a destabilizing actor that threatens security by defying international law and pursuing capabilities that would allow it to develop nuclear weapons

[6412] Even as Iran pledges not to pursue nuclear weapons, its other destabilizing activities including development of mid- and long-range missiles and support to terrorists and insurgents, will continue to pose a threat to the security of the Middle East and the U. S. allies and partners

[6413] The SDF promotes capacity-building initiatives regarding information-gathering abilities and defensive abilities in dispatch destinations, which are required to complete missions while ensuring the security of personnel and units during international peace cooperation activities

[6414] In addition, in order to respond to a variety of environments and prolonged missions, the SDF promotes initiatives to improve the capabilities for transport and deployment and information communication, and to develop a structure of replenishment and medical support for conducting smooth and continuous operations

[6415] The GSDF promotes initiatives to enhance the conditions This is a system adopted by the United Nations in 1994 in order to facilitate agile deployment for U. N. peacekeeping operations

[6416] The system involves member nations registering beforehand the scope of the contribution that they can make, the number of personnel available for dispatch, and the time required for dispatch

[6417] When the United Nations approaches member nations with a request for dispatch based on the registered information, it is up to each country to decide whether to actually dispatch personnel or not

[6418] Furthermore, it states that as countries in the Middle East and Africa undergo political and social change, terrorist groups seek to expand their influence, and internal strife in Syria has become a magnet for global jihad, bringing ongoing spillover effects including an influx of foreign fighters and a flood of refugees into neighboring countries

[6419] In Africa, it mentions that terrorists, criminal organizations and pirates exploit ungoverned and under-governed territory, causing potential for rapidly developing threats, particularly of terrorist attacks in fragile states, that could pose acute challenges to U.S. interests

[6420] The report says that Europe remains the principal partner in promoting global security, particularly in addressing challenges such as persistent unrest and violence in the Middle East and North Africa

[6421] The QDR states that while the United States is willing to undertake security cooperation with Russia, both in the bilateral context and in seeking solutions to regional challenges, Russia’s multi-dimensional defense modernization and actions that violate the sovereignty of neighbors present risks and thus the United States will engage Russia to increase transparency and reduce the risk of military miscalculation

[6422] Concerning the global trends, the report refers to the emergence of international partners with the capacity to play security roles in their respective regions, as well as international cooperation and shared norms of behavior at unprecedented levels of global interconnectedness

[6423] At the same time it also states, that the spread and proliferation of technology offers new tools for state and non-state adversaries such as terrorists to pursue asymmetric approaches in the 21st century operational environment

[6424] Furthermore, the report states that in coming years, countries such as China will continue seeking to counter U.S. strengths using anti-access and area-denial (A2/AD) approaches and by employing other new cyber and space control technologies

[6425] It also says that elements such as cyberspace, space, sophisticated technology, WMD, terrorism and climate change poses additional challenges

[6430] Build security globally: Continue a strong U. S. commitment to shaping world events in order to deter and prevent conflict and to assure the allies and partners of the shared security

[6431] Project power and win decisively: the U.S. Forces deter acts of aggression in one or more theaters by remaining capable of decisively defeating adversaries, while projecting power to provide humanitarian assistance and disaster relief

S. forces could defeat a regional adversary in a large-scale multi-phased campaign, and deny the objectives of—or imposing unacceptable costs on—another region

[6438] The QDR also says that while the force will become smaller, it will become more modern as well, with readiness improving

[6577] Quadrennial Defense Review (QDR

[6578] In March 2014, the Department of Defense released the Quadrennial Defense Review (QDR

[6579] The QDR outlines policies concerning U. S. Forces' capabilities and composition in anticipation of the security environment of the next 20 years

[6580] The United States Code mandates that the Secretary of Defense submits the QDR to the Congress every four years

[6581] The 2014 QDR builds on the 2012 Defense Strategic Guidance and embodies the priorities outlined in it

[6582] The 2014 QDR states that the future international security environment remains uncertain and complicated due to the shifting international balance of power; the greater interaction between states, non-state entities and private citizens; the proliferation of technology; and the rapidly accelerating spread of information

[6583] In addressing this challenging environment, the QDR states that the United States collaborates with allies and partners to accomplish a wide range of goals, and leverages the technological and human capital strengths of the U.S. Forces

[6584] The QDR recognizes that the Asia-Pacific region is increasingly central to global commerce, politics and security

[6585] At the same time, the report points out that defense expenditure in the region continues to rise and countries within the region continue to enhance their military and security capabilities, bringing greater risk that tensions arising from long-standing sovereign disputes or claims to natural resources will spur disruptive competition or erupt into conflict

[6586] In particular, it notes that the rapid pace and comprehensive scope of China’s military modernization continues, combined with a relative lack of transparency and openness regarding both military capabilities and intentions

[6587] In relation to North Korea, the review says that its long-range missile and weapons of mass destruction (WMD) programs, particularly its pursuit of nuclear weapons in violation of international obligations, constitutes a significant threat to peace and stability on the Korean Peninsula and Northeast Asia and is a growing, direct threat to the United States

[6588] As for the Middle East, the report suggests that the sectarian divide is among the sources of trans-national division, while competition for resources will worsen tensions and could escalate into broader conflicts, particularly in fragile states

[6589] The report states that Iran remains a destabilizing actor that threatens security by defying international law and pursing capabilities that would allow it to develop nuclear weapons

[6590] Even as Iran pledges not to pursue nuclear weapons, its other destabilizing activities including development of mid- and long-range missiles and support to terrorists and insurgents, will continue to pose a threat to the security of the Middle East and the U. S. allies and partners

[6591] Furthermore, it states that as countries in the Middle East and Africa undergo political and social change, terrorist groups seek to expand their influence, and internal strife in Syria has become a magnet for global jihad, bringing ongoing spillover effects including an influx of foreign fighters and a flood of refugees into neighboring countries

[6592] In Africa, it mentions that terrorists, criminal organizations and pirates exploit ungoverned and undergoverned territory, causing potential for rapidly developing threats, particularly of terrorist attacks in fragile states, that could pose acute challenges to U. S. interests

[6593] The report says that Europe remains the principal partner in promoting global security, particularly in addressing challenges such as persistent unrest and violence in the Middle East and North Africa

[6594] The QDR states that while the United States is willing to undertake security cooperation with Russia, both in the bilateral context and in seeking solutions to regional challenges, Russia’s multidimensional defense modernization and actions that violate the sovereignty of neighbors present risks and thus the United States will engage Russia to increase transparency and reduce the risk of military miscalculation

[6595] Concerning the global trends, the report refers to the emergence of international partners with the capacity to play security roles in their respective regions, as well as international cooperation and shared norms of behavior at unprecedented levels of global interconnectedness

[6596] At the same time it also states that the spread and proliferation of technology offers new tools for state and non-state adversaries such as terrorists to pursue asymmetric approaches in the 21st century operational environment

[6597] Furthermore, the report states that in coming years, countries such as China will continue seeking to counter U.S. strengths using anti-access and area-denial (A2/AD) approaches and by employing other new cyber and space control technologies

[6598] It also says that elements such as cyberspace, space, sophisticated technology, WMD, terrorism and climate change poses additional challenges

[6671] To date, the MOD has been endeavoring to achieve greater efficiency by extending the interval between periodic maintenance and to implement and expand the use of PBL (Performance Based Logistics), which is a new form of contract

[6672] Having made adequate efforts to ensure that safety is not compromised, greater efficiency is being sought by extending the interval between periodic maintenance checks of defense equipment such as fixed-wing aircraft, helicopters, and Patriot missiles

[6673] For example, cost reductions have been achieved by extending the interval between overhauls for ten types of gas turbine engine on naval vessels from 8,000 hours, as it was prior, to 10,000 hours; and increasing the interval between progressive aircraft reworks of P-3C maritime patrol aircraft (P-3C) from 40 to 48 months

[6674] PBL, which involves paying compensation for achieving equipment performance in terms of availability ratio and safety, is a contract method that has achieved positive outcomes

[6933] Maintain the capability to deter and defeat attacks on the United States

[6935] Build security globally: Continue a strong U. S. commitment to shaping world events in order to deter and prevent conflict and to assure the allies and partners of the shared security

[6936] Project power and win decisively: the U. S. Forces deter acts of aggression in one or more theaters by remaining capable of decisively defeating adversaries, while projecting power to provide humanitarian assistance and disaster relief

[7103] Enhancement of Medical Functions Introduction of a Four-year Nursing Course at the National Defense Medical College The MOD and the SDF have been facing an increasing need to train high-quality nurses equipped with the expertise and skills required to fully respond to the diversification and internationalization of duties, and the sophistication and complication of medical technology, and also equipped with well-rounded humanity and the ability to make accurate judgments

[7104] For this reason, a four-year “nursing program” was introduced for the training of public health/registered nurses at the National Defense Medical College, Faculty of Nursing, in April

[7105] The nursing program consists of two courses, one for education and training of nurses who will be SDF officers (1 year course, 75 attendees; hereinafter “SDF officers’ course”), and the other for education and training of nurses who will be technical officers working at the affiliated hospitals (1 year course, 45 attendees; hereinafter “technical officials’ course”

[7106] The SDF officers’ course will also provide education and training as required for becoming senior SDF officers

[7107] Among graduates of the nurse training program, those who have completed the SDF officers’ course will be assigned to work at SDF medical units and SDF hospitals after finishing the necessary training at the Officer Candidate Schools, while those who have completed the technical officers’ course will be assigned to work at the National Defense Medical College Hospital, which deals with cases that require advanced medical technology

[7108] SDF medical personnel are required to have appropriate discernment and quality as SDF personnel according to the respective ranks and positions and display leadership in the medical field

[7109] Furthermore, they are also required to have the ability as a clinician in comprehensive medicine

[7110] Furthermore, they are engaged at all times toward the objective of maintaining and increasing their abilities

[7111] However, the fill rate of SDF medical personnel is currently at a low level, and in particular, it is considerably low for the middle level personnel who are supposed to play a central role in international peace cooperation activities

[7112] Such low sufficiency is caused by medical officers leaving the SDF, one of the major reasons of which is the lack of opportunity to engage in training and medical practice

[7113] The MOD and the SDF will make efforts to prevent medical officers from leaving the SDF by providing them with more opportunities to engage in training and medical practice so that they can acquire, maintain, and improve specialist skills, while increasing motivation for their work and loyalty to their organization

[7114] At the same time, the MOD and SDF will take various measures as soon as possible to train medical officers who are capable of performing diverse duties properly

[7137] Quadrennial Defense Review (QDR

[7138] In March 2014, the Department of Defense released the Quadrennial Defense Review (QDR

[7139] The QDR outlines policies concerning U. S. Forces' capabilities and composition in anticipation of the security environment of the next 20 years

[7140] The United States Code mandates that the Secretary of Defense submits the QDR to the Congress every four years

[7141] The 2014 QDR builds on the 2012 Defense Strategic Guidance and embodies the priorities outlined in it

[7142] The 2014 QDR states that the future international security environment remains uncertain and complicated due to the shifting international balance of power; the greater interaction between states, non-state entities and private citizens; the proliferation of technology; and the rapidly accelerating spread of information

[7143] In addressing this challenging environment, the QDR states that the United States collaborates with allies and partners to accomplish a wide range of goals, and leverages the technological and human capital strengths of the U.S. Forces

[7144] The QDR recognizes that the Asia-Pacific region is increasingly central to global commerce, politics and security

[7145] At the same time, the report points out that defense expenditure in the region continues to rise and countries within the region continue to enhance their military and security capabilities, bringing greater risk that tensions arising from long-standing sovereign disputes or claims to natural resources will spur disruptive competition or erupt into conflict

[7146] In particular, it notes that the rapid pace and comprehensive scope of China’s military modernization continues, combined with a relative lack of transparency and openness regarding both military capabilities and intentions

[7147] In relation to North Korea, the review says that its long-range missile and weapons of mass destruction (WMD) programs, particularly its pursuit of nuclear weapons in violation of international obligations, constitutes a significant threat to peace and stability on the Korean Peninsula and Northeast Asia and is a growing, direct threat to the United States

[7148] As for the Middle East, the report suggests that the sectarian divide is among the sources of transnational division, while competition for resources will worsen tensions and could escalate into broader conflicts, particularly in fragile states

[7149] The report states that Iran remains a destabilizing actor that threatens security by defying international law and pursuing capabilities that would allow it to develop nuclear weapons

[7150] Even as Iran pledges not to pursue nuclear weapons, its other destabilizing activities including development of mid- and long-range missiles and support to terrorists and insurgents, will continue to pose a threat to the security of the Middle East and the U. S. allies and partners

[7151] Furthermore, it states that as countries in the Middle East and Africa undergo political and social change, terrorist groups seek to expand their influence, and internal strife in Syria has become a magnet for global jihad, bringing ongoing spillover effects including an influx of foreign fighters and a flood of refugees into neighboring countries

[7152] In Africa, it mentions that terrorists, criminal organizations and pirates exploit ungoverned and under-governed territory, causing potential for rapidly developing threats, particularly of terrorist attacks in fragile states, that could pose acute challenges to U. S. interests

[7153] The report says that Europe remains the principal partner in promoting global security, particularly in addressing challenges such as persistent unrest and violence in the Middle East and North Africa

[7154] The QDR states that while the United States is willing to undertake security cooperation with Russia, both in the bilateral context and in seeking solutions to regional challenges, Russia’s multidimensional defense modernization and actions that violate the sovereignty of neighbors present risks and thus the United States will engage Russia to increase transparency and reduce the risk of military miscalculation

[7155] Concerning the global trends, the report refers to the emergence of international partners with the capacity to play security roles in their respective regions, as well as international cooperation and shared norms of behavior at unprecedented levels of global interconnectedness

[7156] At the same time it also states that the spread and proliferation of technology offers new tools for state and non-state adversaries such as terrorists to pursue asymmetric approaches in the 21st century operational environment

[7157] Furthermore, the report states that in coming years, countries such as China will continue seeking to counter U.S. strengths using anti-access and area-denial (A2/AD) approaches and by employing other new cyber and space control technologies

[7158] It also says that elements such as cyberspace, space, sophisticated technology, WMD, terrorism and climate change poses additional challenges

[7189] The 2014 QDR emphasizes the following three pillars, which are interdependent and mutually reinforcing, in order to embody priorities outlined in the 2012 Defense Strategic Guidance including rebalancing toward the Asia-Pacific region and strong commitment to stability in Europe and the Middle East

[7190] Protect the Homeland

[7191] Maintain the capability to deter and defeat attacks on the United States

[7192] Protection of the homeland includes assisting U.S. civil authorities in protecting U. S. airspace, shores, and borders, and in responding effectively to domestic disasters

[7193] Build security globally: Continue a strong U. S. commitment to shaping world events in order to deter and prevent conflict and to assure the allies and partners of the shared security

[7194] Project power and win decisively: The U. S. Forces deter acts of aggression in one or more theaters by remaining capable of decisively defeating adversaries, while projecting power to provide humanitarian assistance and disaster relief

[7195] The QDR states that across the three pillars, the U. S. Forces are capable of simultaneously implementing the following undertakings, and if deterrence fails at any given time, U. S. forces could defeat a regional adversary in a large-scale multi-phased campaign, and deny the objectives of—or imposing unacceptable costs on —another aggressor in another region

[7196] Defending homeland 2) Conducting sustained, distributed counterterrorist operations 3) Deterring aggression and assuring allies through forward presence and engagement in multiple regions

[7197] Deterring aggression and assuring allies through forward presence and engagement in multiple regions

[7198] The 2010 QDR stated that the U. S. Forces possess the capability of countering attacks by two countries while also being able to conduct a wide range of operations

[7199] The 2012 Defense Strategic Guidance states that the United States maintains forces that are able to fully deny a capable state’s aggressive objectives in one region while being capable of denying the objectives of – or imposing unacceptable costs on – an opportunistic aggressor in a second region

[7200] Furthermore, in order to achieve the three pillars, the Department of Defense seeks innovative approaches to how to fight, how to posture the force, and how to leverage the asymmetric strengths and technological advantages

[7201] More specifically, the QDR mentions positioning additional forward-deployed naval forces in critical areas, such as the Asia-Pacific region, and deploying new combinations of ships, aviation assets, and crisis response forces

[7202] Rebalancing of the Joint Force Given major changes in the United States security environment including geopolitical changes, changes in modern warfare, and changes in the fiscal environment, the 2014 QDR states that the Department of Defense will rebalance the Joint Force for a broad spectrum of conflict, rebalance and maintain the presence and posture abroad, and rebalance capability, capacity and readiness

[7203] The QDR also says that while the force will become smaller, it will become more modern as well, with readiness improving

[7204] Furthermore, it states that particularly in an era of reduced budget and other resources, the Department will redouble its efforts to protect key capability areas listed below, that are most closely aligned to the pillars of the defense strategy

[7240] Nuclear Strategy While U. S. President Obama aims to realize a world without nuclear weapons, he notes that this will not be realized in the near future, and indicates the need to maintain a nuclear deterrent as long as nuclear weapons exist

[7241] The Nuclear Posture Review (NPR), which was released in April 2010, indicates that the nuclear security environment is changing and nuclear terrorism and nuclear proliferation are an imminent threat today

[7242] Furthermore, it points to the necessity of working on the issue of ensuring strategic stability with existing nuclear powers, in particular Russia and China

[7243] The NPR presents five key objectives based on awareness of this security environment: preventing nuclear proliferation and nuclear terrorism; reducing the role of U. S. nuclear weapons; maintaining strategic deterrence and stability at reduced nuclear force levels; strengthening regional deterrence and reassuring U. S. allies and partners; and sustaining a safe, secure, and effective nuclear arsenal
